other.about: Small bodies up close (track SB). A belt, ring or cloud stays a probability field until one member is looked at; that member then resolves, from the seed and its address alone, into a definite body: what it is made of, the type read off that, rubble pile or monolith, single, contact binary or separated pair, its spin, its figure and a short history. Every number below is editable and cited; the citations are in docs/citations.md (rows SB-*) and the simplifications in docs/fudges.md (rows SB-*).

makeup.about: Grain densities are read from the master data sheet (mixtures formation-metal, -rock, -carbon, -water). A member's makeup scatters around its cloud's mean (metal, rock, carbon, ice) by a log-normal factor per share, then renormalises. Fragments of a differentiated parent come mostly from one layer.

ice.about: Water ice survives on the surface where the blackbody temperature 278.6 K L^0.25 / sqrt(a) is below this (sublimation over billions of years).

types.about: The type is a label read off the member's makeup and surface, never an input. Albedos are survey means.

collisions.about: Disruption lifetime of a main-belt body t = t0 (R / 1 m)^0.5 (Farinella et al. 1998 eq. 14 and 15), scaled by how crowded and fast the member's cloud is against the main belt. A body disrupted within its system's age has re-accumulated as a rubble pile if self-gravity, not strength, holds it (D above the strength-gravity transition near 0.3 km, Benz and Asphaug 1999).

yorp.about: Sunlight spins small bodies up or down (YORP). The time to change the spin by its own size grows as D^2 a^2 / L. Where it has had time, spins are spread flat in frequency up to the spin barrier and rubble piles shed mass into pairs.

spin.about: Bodies YORP has not reached keep a Maxwellian spread of spin rates from their collisional past. Monoliths below the transition may spin faster than the barrier.

pairs.about: Shares among bodies YORP has worked on (near-Earth asteroids over 200 m by radar and light curves), among cold, primordial discs (gentle mergers, like Arrokoth), and for large bodies with impact moons.

figure.about: Large bodies relax to the figure of a spinning fluid (Maclaurin, then Jacobi); small ones keep an irregular figure held by strength or friction. Round above roughly 600 km for rock and 400 km for ice.

weathering.about: Solar wind darkens and reddens an exposed surface in about a million years at 1 AU, slower as a^2.
